## Resources

-   the [Origin-destination data with stplanr](https://docs.ropensci.org/stplanr/articles/stplanr-od.html) manual,

-   the [Modelling Population Flows Using Spatial Interaction Models](https://rpubs.com/adam_dennett/376877) tutorial, and

## Commuting data and networks

This the same data and the same data preparation we did for the [network analysis practical](https://etranos.info/urban_analytics_city_science/src/network_analysis.html). Please follow the below workflow, which you should already be familiar with. Once the data preparation is done, we will model these commuting flows.

For this tutorial we will use travel to work data from the 2011 UK Census. The data is available [online](http://wicid.ukdataservice.ac.uk/cider/wicid/downloads.php?wicid_Session=742d61be88b0614c3982455e542bc776), but it requires an academic login. After you log in, download the **WU03UK** element, save the .csv on your working directory under a `/data` directory and unzip it. We will use the:

> Location of usual residence and place of work by method of travel to work

for

> Census Merged local authority districts in England and Wales, Council areas in Scotland, Local government districts in Northern Ireland.

The below code loads the data.

```{r data load}

path.data <- paste0(path, "/data/wu03uk_v3/wu03uk_v3.csv")
commuting <- read_csv(path.data)
commuting
```

You might have observe some weird codes (OD0000001, OD0000002, OD0000003 and OD0000004). With some simple Google searching we can find the [2011 Census Origin-Destination Data User Guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/file?uri=/census/2011census/2011censusdata/originanddestinationdata/secureoriginanddestinationtables/2011censusoduserguide_tcm77-383888.pdf), which indicates that these codes do not refer to local authorities:

-   OD0000001 = Mainly work at or from home

-   OD0000002 = Offshore installation

-   OD0000003 = No fixed place

-   OD0000004 = Outside UK

For the sake of simplicity we will remove these non-geographical nodes.

```{r drop non_la, include=TRUE, results= 'asis', message=FALSE}
non.la <- c("OD0000001", "OD0000002", "OD0000003", "OD0000004")
commuting <- commuting %>% 
  filter(!`Area of workplace` %in% non.la)
```

check the `%in%` [operator](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/match.html).

Now let's do some clean-up of the `commuting` data frame. Let's remind ourselves how the data look like

We are keeping the English and Wales local authorities by keeping the observations with a local authority code starting from E (for England) and W (for Wales).

```{r la.cleanup2, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE}
commuting <- commuting %>% filter(startsWith(`Area of usual residence`, "E") |
                                  startsWith(`Area of usual residence`, "W")) %>% 
                           filter(startsWith(`Area of workplace`, "E") |
                                  startsWith(`Area of workplace`, "W")) %>% 
  glimpse()
```

We can also see we many rows we dropped with `glimpse()`.

It is very important to distinguish between intra- and inter-local authority flows. In network analysis terms, these are the values we find on the diagonal of an adjacency matrix and refer to the commuting flows within a specific local authority or between different ones. For this exercise we are dropping the intra-local authority flows. Although not used here, we also create a new object with the intra-local authority flows.

```{r la.cleanup3, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE}
commuting.intra <- commuting %>%
  filter(`Area of usual residence` == `Area of workplace`)
commuting <- commuting %>%
  filter(`Area of usual residence` != `Area of workplace`) %>% 
  glimpse()
```

Please note the constant use of `glimpse()` to keep control of how many observations we have and check if we missed anything.

Also, take a note of the `commuting` object, which includes multiple types of commuting flows. Therefore, we will build $3$ different networks:

1.  one for all the commuting flows

2.  one only for train flows

3.  one only for bicycle flows.

```{r seperate commuting objects, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE}

commuting.all <- commuting %>%
  select(`Area of usual residence`,
                `Area of workplace`,
                `All categories: Method of travel to work`) %>%
  rename(o = `Area of usual residence`,     # Area of usual residence is annoyingly
         d = `Area of workplace`,           # long, so I am renaiming theses columns
         weight = `All categories: Method of travel to work`)

# just FYI this is how you could have achieved the same output using base R
# instead of dplyr of the tidyverse ecosystem
# commuting.all <- commuting[,1:3]
# names(commuting.all)[1] <- "o"
# names(commuting.all)[2] <- "d"
# names(commuting.all)[3] <- "weight"

commuting.train <- commuting %>%
  select(`Area of usual residence`,
         `Area of workplace`,
         `All categories: Method of travel to work`,
         `Train`) %>%
  rename(o = `Area of usual residence`,
         d = `Area of workplace`,
         weight = `All categories: Method of travel to work`) %>%
  # The below code drops all the lines with 0 train flows in order to exclude
  # these edges from the network.
  filter(Train!=0)

commuting.bicycle <- commuting %>%
  select(`Area of usual residence`,
                `Area of workplace`,
                `All categories: Method of travel to work`,
                `Bicycle`) %>%
  rename(o = `Area of usual residence`,
         d = `Area of workplace`,
         weight = `All categories: Method of travel to work`) %>%
  # The below code drops all the lines with 0 bicycle flows in order to exclude
  # these edges from the network.
  filter(Bicycle!=0)
```

Unless you know the local authority codes by hard, it might be useful to also add the corresponding local authority names. These can be easily obtained from the [ONS](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/datasets/ons::cmlad-dec-2011-super-generalised-clipped-boundaries-gb/explore?showTable=true). The below code directly downloads a `GeoJSON` file with the local authorities in England and Wales. If you don't know what a `GeoJSON` file is, have a look [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GeoJSON). Boundary data can also be obtained by [UK Data Service](https://borders.ukdataservice.ac.uk/easy_download.html).

For the time being we are only interested in the local authority names and codes. We will use the spatial object later.  

**Tip**: the below code downloads the `GeoJSON` file over the web. If you want to run the code multiple times, it might be faster to download the file ones, save it on your hard drive and the point this location to `st_read()`.

```{r la1, include=TRUE, results= 'hide', message=FALSE}
la <-st_read("https://services1.arcgis.com/ESMARspQHYMw9BZ9/arcgis/rest/services/CMLAD_Dec_2011_SGCB_GB_2022/FeatureServer/0/query?outFields=*&where=1%3D1&f=geojson")
glimpse(la) 

la.names <- as.data.frame(la) %>% 
  select(cmlad11cd, cmlad11nm)    # all we need is the LA names and codes
```

## Spatial interaction modelling

Let's now move to model these flows. If you remember the basic Gravity model is defined as following:

$$T_{ij} = k \displaystyle \frac{V_i^\lambda M_j^\alpha}{D_{ij}^\beta}$$

And if we take the logarithms of both sides of the equation we can transform the Gravity model to something which looks like a linear model:

$$lnT_{ij} = lnk + \lambda lnV_i + \alpha lnM_j - \beta lnD_{ij}$$

The above transformed equation can be estimated as a linear model if we assume that $y = lnT_{ij}$, $c = lnk$, $x_1 = lnV_i$, $a_1 = \lambda$ etc. Hence, we can use OLS to estimate the following:

$$lnT_{ij} = lnk + \lambda lnV_i + \alpha lnM_j - \beta lnD_{ij} + e_{ij}$$

This is what is known as the log-log transformation.

There are a number of issues with such an approach though. Most importantly, our dependent variable is not continuous, but instead a discrete, positive variable (there are no flows of -324.56 people!). Therefore we need to employ an appropriate estimator and this is what the Poisson regression does. Briefly, if we exponentiate both sides, the above equation can be written as:

$$T_{ij} = e^{lnk + \lambda lnV_i + \alpha lnM_j - \beta lnD_{ij}}$$ The above is in the form of the Poisson regression. So, we are interested in modelling *not* the mean $T_{ij}$ drawn from a normally distributed $T$, but, instead, the mean $T_{ij}$, which is the average of the all the flows (i.e. counts) between any $i$ and $j$. For more details about the Poisson regression have a look at  [@roback2021beyond](https://bookdown.org/roback/bookdown-bysh/ch-poissonreg.html#initial-models). For this practical we will estimate the commuting flows using both OLS and Poisson regressions.

But before we get into the estimation we need to build a data frame, which includes all the necessary variables. These are the origin-destination flows $T$ between $i$ and $j$, the distance $dist$ between $i$ and $j$ and the characteristics $V$ and $M$ of origin $i$ and destinations $j$ that we believe *push* and *pull* individuals to commute.

```{r si data, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# we use the `SpatialPosition` package and the `CreateDistMatrix()` function to
# calculate a distance matrix for all local authorities,
la.d <- CreateDistMatrix(la, la, longlat = T)

# we use as column and row name the local authority codes
rownames(la.d) <- la$cmlad11cd
colnames(la.d) <- la$cmlad11cd

# This is a matrix of the distances between *all* local authorities. We then use
# the function as.data.frame.table() to convert this matrix to a data frame each
# line of which represents an origin-destination pair.
la.d <- as.data.frame.table(la.d, responseName = "value")
glimpse(la.d)

# Please note that the elements of the diagonal are present in this distance matrix.
```

If you want to check that the distances we are correct, use Google maps to calculate the distance between E41000001 (Middlesbrough) and E41000002 (Hartlepool). Remember that the la.d is expressed in meters.

What is missing here? Do you remember the intra-zone commuting flows? E.g. the commuters that live and work in Bristol? We had removed these from the network analysis and visualisation element. Because we don't have information about the distances of the intra-zone commutes, we will exclude them from this analysis.

```{r si data2, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
la.d <- la.d %>%
  filter(Var1 != Var2) %>% 
  glimpse()
```

What we want to do is to match the data frame with all the distances with the commuting flows data frame. To do that we will (1) create a new data frame for the origin-destination pair and (2) match the two data frames.

```{r si data3, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

la.d <- la.d %>% 
  mutate(ij.code = paste(Var1, Var2, sep = "_")) %>% 
  glimpse()

commuting <- commuting %>% 
  mutate(ij.code = paste(`Area of usual residence`,
                          `Area of workplace`,
                           sep = "_")) %>% 
  glimpse()
```

Before we perform the match, keep a note of how many observations both data frames have in order to check if we loose any observations during the matching. As you can see the commuting data frame has less observations than the la.d one, which includes all the possible origin-destination pairs.

What does it mean? That for some origin-destination pairs there are no commuting flows, which of course makes sense. We need to include these pairs with $flow = 0$ in our data though because the lack of commuting flows **is not** missing data!

```{r si data4, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

commuting.si <- full_join(la.d, commuting, by = "ij.code") %>% 
  glimpse()

# Some variables are repetitive or need name change
commuting.si <- commuting.si %>% 
  rename(i = Var1,
         j = Var2,
         distance = value) %>% 
  select(-`Area of usual residence`,
         -`Area of workplace`) %>% 
  glimpse()

# Let's see if we have any missing values
sapply(commuting.si, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
```

There are quite a few. What does it mean? That there are no commuting flows for these origin-destination pairs and,therefore, were excluded from the origin commuting data set we downloaded. So, we are going to replace these $NAs$ with $0s$.

```{r si data5, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
commuting.si <- commuting.si %>% 
  replace(., is.na(.), 0)
```

Now let's bring data for some $i$ and $j$ characteristics that we believe that affect commuting. I have prepared such a small data set from the census, which includes resident population and working populations as *push* and *pull* variables. These data have been obtained by [nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/published/census/odexplorer.asp).

As you can see, there are two columns with LA codes: `la.code.st` and `Merging.Local.Authority.Code`. Because Local Authority codes and definitions change overtime, I had to do some pre-processing. We will use the `Merging.Local.Authority.Code` to merge with our flow data, but there are 6 Local Authorities that I couldn't much. Later down the pipeline, I will drop these cases.   

```{r si ij data, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# To avoid issues with read_csv() reading directly from Dropbox, we use a 
# tempfile trick. First, an empty temp file is created with tempfile(). Then, we 
# use download.file() to download the Dropbox file to this temp file. Finally, 
# we read the temp file using read_csv().

temp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download.file(
  "https://www.dropbox.com/s/0ym88p8quwaiyau/data_workplace.csv?dl=1",
  destfile = temp,
  mode = "wb"
)
data.workplace <- readr::read_csv(temp)

# Alternatively, you could read directly from Dropbox using read_csv() 
#data.workplace <- read_csv("https://www.dropbox.com/s/0ym88p8quwaiyau/data_workplace.csv?dl=1")

# Important Dropbox trick: to use the link that Dropbox provides to share a 
# file in an .Rmd replace dl=0 with dl=1 at the end of the link.

temp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download.file(
  "https://www.dropbox.com/s/09d7v5cm6ov3ioz/data_resident.csv?dl=1",
  destfile = temp,
  mode = "wb"
)
data.resident <- readr::read_csv(temp)

# Alternatively, you could read directly from Dropbox using read_csv() 
#data.resident <- read_csv("https://www.dropbox.com/s/09d7v5cm6ov3ioz/data_resident.csv?dl=1")

commuting.si <- commuting.si %>% 
  left_join(data.resident, by = c('i' = 'Merging.Local.Authority.Code')) %>% 
  left_join(data.workplace, by = c('j' = 'Merging.Local.Authority.Code')) 
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** are there any redundant columns? Can you remove them?
```

Before we start modelling these flows, let's plot our variables.

```{r si.plots, include=TRUE, results= 'asis', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
ggplot(commuting.si, aes(x=distance,
                         y=`All categories: Method of travel to work`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm)

ggplot(commuting.si, aes(x=resident,
                         y=`All categories: Method of travel to work`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm)

ggplot(commuting.si, aes(x=workplace,
                         y=`All categories: Method of travel to work`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method=lm)
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** What do you take from these graphs?
```

Let's try now to model these flows. We will start with a simple OLS to estimate the above specifications. Please pay attention to the small trick we did. Because there are non-materialised origin-destination pairs (i.e. with 0 flows), we added a small value ($0.5$) in the dependent variable. Otherwise we will receive an error as the logarithm of $0$ is not defined.

```{r si_ols, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

ols.model <- lm(log(`All categories: Method of travel to work`+.5) ~
                  log(distance) + log(resident) + log(workplace),
                data = commuting.si)

# To see the model output you can use the summary() function.
summary(ols.model)
```

So, the OLS regression estimated the four parameters:

-   $lnk = 7.968$
-   $\beta = -1.840$
-   $\lambda = 0.514$
-   $\alpha = -0.852$

Let's estimate now our model using a Poisson regression. Given that we don't take the logarithm of the dependent variable, there is no need to add $0.5$.

```{r si_poisson, include=TRUE, results= 'markup', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}

glm.model <- glm((`All categories: Method of travel to work`)~
                   log(distance) + log(resident) + log(workplace),
                 family = poisson(link = "log"), data = commuting.si)
summary(glm.model)
```

The following parameter1 have been estimated

-   $lnk = 11.664$
-   $\beta = -1.816$
-   $\lambda = 0.318$
-   $\alpha = 0.820$

As you can see the differences are rather small.

The `stargazer` package I use below creates elegant regression tables. Replace `type = "html"` with `type = "text"` to have be able to read the results using the .Rmd document. the "html" option is useful for when knitting the script to an .html document.

```{r stargazer, include=TRUE, results= 'asis', message=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
stargazer(ols.model, glm.model, type = "html")
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Can you interpret the regression results?
```

## Constrained spatial interaction models

The Poisson (and the OLS) model we just estimated is an *unconstrained* spatial interaction model. Nothing forces the predicted flows to be consistent with what we already know about the system. For example, if we sum the predicted flows for all the commuters who live in Bristol, there is no guarantee that we will get the actual number of Bristol residents who commute to another local authority.

But very often we *do* know these totals. The census tells us how many people live in each local authority and commute elsewhere ($O_i$, the *origin* totals) and how many jobs are taken by commuters in each local authority ($D_j$, the *destination* totals). What we do not know, or what we want to predict, is how these totals are *distributed*, i.e. who commutes where. This is what *constrained* spatial interaction models do [@wilson1971family]. There are four types:

| Type                   | What is fixed            | $\sum_j T_{ij}$ | $\sum_i T_{ij}$ |
|------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Unconstrained          | nothing                  | free            | free            |
| Production-constrained | origin totals, $O_i$     | $= O_i$         | free            |
| Attraction-constrained | destination totals, $D_j$| free            | $= D_j$         |
| Doubly constrained     | both                     | $= O_i$         | $= D_j$         |

In this section we will estimate the production-constrained and the doubly constrained models for the same commuting flows and compare them with the unconstrained one we estimated above. The attraction-constrained model is the mirror image of the production-constrained one and you will estimate it as a task at the end.

### Production-constrained model

The production-constrained model is defined as:

$$T_{ij} = A_i \, O_i \, M_j^\alpha \, D_{ij}^{-\beta} \qquad \text{where} \qquad A_i = \frac{1}{\sum_j M_j^\alpha D_{ij}^{-\beta}}$$

Compare it with the unconstrained model. The origin characteristic $V_i^\lambda$ has been replaced by the *known* origin total $O_i$ and the new term $A_i$ is a *balancing factor*, which makes sure that the predicted flows from each origin add up to $O_i$, i.e. $\sum_j T_{ij} = O_i$. Please note that we do not estimate $\lambda$ any more. We still estimate $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

An important by-product: $1/A_i = \sum_j M_j^\alpha D_{ij}^{-\beta}$ is the gravity-based *accessibility* of origin $i$ (do you remember the accessibility indicators from the lecture?). We will come back to this below.


### Preparing the data

Good news: we do not need to change the format of the data. We keep working with the long format, in which each line is an origin-destination pair, and we estimate the constrained models with a Poisson regression, as we did above. The below code prepares a data frame for this. Pay attention to the comments.

```{r constrained_data}
# This package allows us to estimate generalised linear models with a sparse
# matrix of dummy variables. See below why we need it. If you do not have it, run
# install.packages("MatrixModels")
library(MatrixModels)

# First, we keep only the English and Welsh local authorities, as we do not have
# commuting flows for Scotland and Northern Ireland, and we simplify the data
# frame. Note the as.character(), because i and j might be factors.
commuting.c <- commuting.si %>%
  mutate(i = as.character(i),
         j = as.character(j)) %>%
  filter(str_detect(i, "^[EW]"), str_detect(j, "^[EW]")) %>%
  rename(flow = `All categories: Method of travel to work`) %>%
  select(i, j, flow, distance, resident, workplace)

# Do we have any missing values? We want this to be 0, but we have quite a few.
sum(is.na(commuting.c))

# Which variables are they in? These are the resident and workplace populations,
# which come from the census data we joined above.
colSums(is.na(commuting.c))

# Which local authorities do not have such data? An origin without resident
# population or a destination without workplace population.
missing.la <- unique(c(commuting.c$i[is.na(commuting.c$resident)],
                       commuting.c$j[is.na(commuting.c$workplace)]))

la.names %>% filter(cmlad11cd %in% missing.la)

# For the constrained models we need a *complete* set of origins and destinations,
# otherwise the totals O and D would not be consistent. So, we remove all the
# pairs which involve these local authorities, either as origins or as destinations.
commuting.c <- commuting.c %>%
  filter(!i %in% missing.la, !j %in% missing.la)

# Now we should be fine.
sum(is.na(commuting.c))

# The local authority codes. We turn the origin (i) and the destination (j) into
# factors with the same levels, as glm() will create one dummy variable for each level.
codes <- sort(unique(c(commuting.c$i, commuting.c$j)))
commuting.c <- commuting.c %>%
  mutate(i = factor(i, levels = codes),
         j = factor(j, levels = codes))

length(codes)      # number of local authorities
nrow(commuting.c)  # number of origin-destination pairs

# The known totals. O: commuters by origin, D: commuters by destination. Please note
# that they only include commuters who work in a *different* local authority, as
# there are no intra-zonal flows in our data.
O <- tapply(commuting.c$flow, commuting.c$i, sum)
D <- tapply(commuting.c$flow, commuting.c$j, sum)

# A good sanity check: the total of the origins must be equal to the total of
# the destinations.
c(sum(O), sum(D))
```

### Estimating the production-constrained model

How do we estimate $\alpha$ and $\beta$ when the balancing factor $A_i$ is part of the model? Remember that the unconstrained model is, after taking logarithms, a linear model:

$$\ln T_{ij} = \ln A_i + \ln O_i + \alpha \ln M_j - \beta \ln D_{ij}$$

Here, $\ln A_i + \ln O_i$ is a different constant for each origin. Therefore, we can estimate the model with the Poisson regression we already know, by simply adding a *dummy variable for each origin*, which will absorb this term. This is why this model is also known as a Poisson model with *origin fixed effects*. A nice property of the Poisson regression is that, when it includes such dummies, the predicted flows of each origin add up *exactly* to the observed ones. In other words, the constraint is satisfied by construction.

Please note that the `0 +` in the formula removes the common intercept, so that we get one dummy for each origin.

We have around $350$ origins and more than $100,000$ origin-destination pairs. A model matrix with a dummy variable for each origin is huge, but it is almost all zeros. The base `glm()` function stores all these zeros and, as a result, it is very slow for this kind of models (it can take many minutes). The function `glm4()` of the `MatrixModels` package has almost exactly the same syntax, but with the argument `sparse = TRUE` it stores only the non-zero values. It estimates the same model in about a second. The `TOL` argument is the convergence tolerance, which we make stricter than the default so that the constraints are satisfied with high precision.

```{r production_constrained}
prod.glm <- glm4(flow ~ 0 + i + log(workplace) + log(distance),
                 family = poisson(link = "log"), data = commuting.c,
                 sparse = TRUE, control = list(TOL = 1e-7))

# We do not want to print the coefficients of all the origin dummies.
# The last two coefficients are alpha (workplace) and minus beta (distance).
tail(coef(prod.glm), 2)
```

Check that the model does what it promises. The predicted flows from each origin should add up to $O_i$, while there is no such guarantee for the destinations.

```{r production_check}
# The largest difference between predicted and observed origin totals.
max(abs(tapply(fitted(prod.glm), commuting.c$i, sum) - O))

# And the same for the destination totals.
max(abs(tapply(fitted(prod.glm), commuting.c$j, sum) - D))
```

If you are familiar with discrete choice models, this is the same as a multinomial logit model of the choice of destination for the commuters of each origin.

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Compare the estimates of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the ones from the Poisson regression above. Are they similar? Why do you think that this is (or is not) the case?
```

### Doubly constrained model

If we know both the origin and the destination totals, we can use both:

$$T_{ij} = A_i \, B_j \, O_i \, D_j \, D_{ij}^{-\beta}$$

$$A_i = \frac{1}{\sum_j B_j D_j D_{ij}^{-\beta}} \qquad B_j = \frac{1}{\sum_i A_i O_i D_{ij}^{-\beta}}$$

Now all the flows are shaped by the totals and the *only* parameter left to estimate is $\beta$, the friction of distance. Note that $A_i$ depends on $B_j$ and vice versa. We cannot solve them directly, but we can solve them iteratively: start with $B_j = 1$, calculate $A_i$, use it to update $B_j$, and so on, until they stop changing. This is known as the *Furness* (or *iterative proportional fitting*) procedure, which was the traditional way of calibrating these models.

The Poisson regression gives us the same result in one go. This time we add a dummy variable for each origin *and* for each destination. Then, $\ln(A_i O_i)$ is absorbed by the origin dummies and $\ln(B_j D_j)$ by the destination dummies, and the only coefficient left is the one of distance, i.e. $-\beta$. As the origin dummies already play the role of a constant, R drops the dummy of the first destination, which becomes the reference category. This is not a problem, as the predicted flows are not affected.

This is a *big* model, with around $700$ dummies. With the base `glm()` it would take a very long time, but with the sparse matrices of `glm4()` it is again a matter of seconds.

```{r doubly_constrained}
dbl.glm <- glm4(flow ~ 0 + i + j + log(distance),
                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = commuting.c,
                sparse = TRUE, control = list(TOL = 1e-7))

# The estimate for the distance. The coefficient is minus beta.
coef(dbl.glm)["log(distance)"]
```

And the same check as before. This time both the origin and the destination totals should be reproduced.

```{r doubly_check}
max(abs(tapply(fitted(dbl.glm), commuting.c$i, sum) - O))
max(abs(tapply(fitted(dbl.glm), commuting.c$j, sum) - D))
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** What is the difference between the estimate of $\beta$ in the production-constrained and in the doubly constrained model? Why do you think that this is the case? (Hint: in which model does the *distance* have to do all the work of explaining how flows are distributed, and in which is it helped by the destination dummies?)
```

### Comparing the models

Let's now compare the three models. For the unconstrained model we use the Poisson model we estimated earlier. We use three goodness-of-fit measures: the root mean squared error (RMSE), the $R^2$ (here the squared correlation between observed and predicted flows) and the Sørensen index (also known as the Common Part of Commuters, CPC), which is very popular in the flow literature. It is the proportion of commuters who are correctly allocated to their origin-destination pair. It ranges between $0$ (nothing in common) and $1$ (perfect). For more information about the CPC, have a look at @THOMPSON2019102461.

$$CPC = \frac{2\sum_{ij} \min(T_{ij}, \hat{T}_{ij})}{\sum_{ij} T_{ij} + \sum_{ij} \hat{T}_{ij}}$$

```{r compare_models}
# Predictions of the unconstrained model for the same origin-destination pairs
T.unc <- predict(glm.model, newdata = commuting.c, type = "response")

# A function which takes a vector of predicted flows and returns the fit statistics
# and the largest errors in the origin and destination totals.
evaluate <- function(pred) {
  obs <- commuting.c$flow

  tibble(RMSE = sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2)),
         R2 = cor(obs, pred)^2,
         CPC = 2 * sum(pmin(obs, pred)) / (sum(obs) + sum(pred)),
         origin.error = max(abs(tapply(pred, commuting.c$i, sum) - O)),        # largest error in origin totals
         destination.error = max(abs(tapply(pred, commuting.c$j, sum) - D)))   # largest error in destination totals
}

models <- list("Unconstrained" = T.unc,
               "Production-constrained" = fitted(prod.glm),
               "Doubly constrained" = fitted(dbl.glm))

map_dfr(models, evaluate, .id = "Model") %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Comparison of the spatial interaction models")
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Which model fits the data better? Is this surprising? Please note that the constrained models use information from the *observed* flows (the totals), while the unconstrained one doesn't. What does this mean for the comparison? In which cases would it be fair to compare the models like this and in which cases not?

Also, have a look at the last two columns. What do they tell us?
```


```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Tasks**

1. Estimate the *attraction-constrained* model, $T_{ij} = B_j D_j V_i^\lambda D_{ij}^{-\beta}$. Hint: it is the mirror image of the production-constrained one. You need dummies for the destinations (`j`) instead of the origins and the resident population `resident` instead of `workplace`. Which parameters do you estimate? Check that the destination totals are reproduced.

2. So far we used a power function for the distance decay: $D_{ij}^{-\beta}$. Another common choice is the exponential function: $e^{-\beta D_{ij}}$. In the Poisson regression this means that you use `distance` in kilometres instead of `log(distance)`. Estimate the production-constrained model with this specification. Which one fits the data better? (Hint: you can use the `evaluate()` function from above.)

3. (Advanced) Distance is a crude measure of the cost of commuting. Replace the `distance` variable with public transport travel times between the local authorities. You can calculate such a matrix with the [`r5r`](https://ipeagit.github.io/r5r/){target="_blank"} package, which needs OpenStreetMap and public transport (GTFS) data. Does the fit improve?
```

## This is not a Machine Learning introduction...

... but maybe a sneak preview of the philosophy behind *modern* data science approaches to answer computational problems. We are using the `caret` package to:

-   split our data into a training and a test data set

-   train three different models using *only* the training data set: a linear regression (`lm`), the Poisson regression (`glm`) we are already familiar with, and a random forest

-   use the estimated models to make *out-of-sample* predictions using the test data set, i.e. data that the models have never seen

-   compare the predictions with the actual flows and choose the best model.

This is obviously an oversimplification, but it provides a good preview of machine learning frameworks. The key idea is that we do not judge a model by how well it fits the data we used to estimate it, but by how well it predicts *new* data.

It is worth browsing the [`caret`](https://topepo.github.io/caret/) package.

The random forest is the only *real* machine learning model here. It is an ensemble of many decision trees. Each tree splits the data repeatedly using the explanatory variables (e.g. is the distance smaller than x km?) and the final prediction is the average across the trees. Unlike the regressions, we do not tell it what the relationship looks like. It can find non-linear relationships and interactions between variables on its own. We use the `ranger` package, which is a fast implementation of random forests, through `caret`. If you do not have it, run `install.packages("ranger")`.

First, we split the data. We keep $80\%$ of the observations for training and $20\%$ for testing. Please note that we do not change `commuting.si`. Instead, we create a new data frame without missing values and with a shorter name for the number of commuters. The `set.seed()` makes the random split reproducible.

```{r ml_split}
commuting.ml <- commuting.si %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  rename(flow = `All categories: Method of travel to work`)

set.seed(3456)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(commuting.ml$flow, p = .8,
                                  list = FALSE,
                                  times = 1)

commuting.train <- commuting.ml[ trainIndex, ]
commuting.test  <- commuting.ml[-trainIndex, ]

# How many observations in each?
nrow(commuting.train)
nrow(commuting.test)
```

Now we train the models. Please pay attention to the `data` argument: we use the *training* data. `caret` can also do a lot of tuning and resampling, which we skip here with `trainControl(method = "none")` to keep this quick. The random forest has a couple of settings (`mtry`, `min.node.size`), which we fix at reasonable values instead of tuning them. This chunk will take about a minute, mostly because of the random forest.

```{r ml_train}
# No resampling or tuning: each model is estimated once
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "none")

model.lm <- train(flow ~ distance + resident + workplace,
                  data = commuting.train,
                  method = "lm",
                  trControl = ctrl)

model.glm <- train(flow ~ distance + resident + workplace,
                   data = commuting.train,
                   method = "glm",
                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                   trControl = ctrl)

# The random forest has a random element, so we need a seed
set.seed(3456)
model.rf <- train(flow ~ distance + resident + workplace,
                  data = commuting.train,
                  method = "ranger",
                  trControl = ctrl,
                  tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = 2,                 # variables tried at each split
                                        splitrule = "variance",
                                        min.node.size = 5),       # minimum size of the final nodes
                  num.trees = 200,                                # number of trees
                  importance = "impurity")                        # we need this to see which variables matter
```

Then, we use the estimated models to predict the flows for the test data set. We evaluate them with four metrics: the RMSE and the MAE, which are errors measured in commuters (the lower the better); $R^2$, here the squared correlation between observed and predicted flows; and the Sørensen index (CPC) we used above. We use a function, because we will need these metrics more than once. Please note that the linear regression can predict negative flows, which we set to $0$ for the CPC.

```{r ml_metrics}
# A function which takes the observed and the predicted flows and calculates
# the metrics
ml_metrics <- function(obs, pred) {
  tibble(RMSE = sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2)),
         MAE = mean(abs(obs - pred)),
         Rsquared = cor(obs, pred)^2,
         CPC = 2 * sum(pmin(obs, pmax(pred, 0))) / (sum(obs) + sum(pmax(pred, 0))))
}

models.ml <- list("lm" = model.lm,
                  "glm" = model.glm,
                  "Random forest" = model.rf)

# The predictions for the test data. predict() works in the same way for all the models.
predictions <- map(models.ml, ~ predict(.x, commuting.test))

# The metrics for the test data
map_dfr(predictions, ~ ml_metrics(commuting.test$flow, .x), .id = "Model") %>%
  select(Model, Rsquared, RMSE, MAE, CPC) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Out-of-sample performance (test data)")
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Which model would you choose? Which model predicts best on the *test* data? Why do you think this is the case?

And why does it matter that the test data were *not* used to estimate the models? What would have happened to the results if we had trained the models using all the data?
```

The plots below show the actual versus the predicted flows for the test data. A perfect model would have all the points on the red line. Because most flows are small and a few are very large, we use a transformation of the axes which is similar to a logarithmic one, but works with zeros and negative values.

```{r ml_plots}
tibble(y = commuting.test$flow,
       lm = predictions$lm,
       glm = predictions$glm,
       `Random forest` = predictions$`Random forest`) %>%
  pivot_longer(-y, names_to = "Model", values_to = "y_hat") %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = names(models.ml))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = y, y = y_hat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "red") +    # perfect predictions
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "pseudo_log") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "pseudo_log") +
  facet_wrap(~ Model) +
  labs(x = "Actual flows", y = "Predicted flows")
```

Now, let's see why we need a test data set. We can also use the models to predict the data that we used to *train* them. Compare how well each model performs on the training and the test data.

```{r ml_overfitting}
# The same metrics for the training data
predictions.train <- map(models.ml, ~ predict(.x, commuting.train))

bind_rows(
  map2_dfr(predictions.train, names(predictions.train),
           ~ ml_metrics(commuting.train$flow, .x) %>% mutate(Model = .y, Data = "Training")),
  map2_dfr(predictions, names(predictions),
           ~ ml_metrics(commuting.test$flow, .x) %>% mutate(Model = .y, Data = "Test"))
) %>%
  select(Model, Data, Rsquared, RMSE, CPC) %>%
  arrange(Model, desc(Data)) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Performance on the training and the test data")
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Which model performs a lot better on the training than on the test data? This is called *overfitting*: the model memorises the noise of the training data instead of learning the general pattern. Why do you think that more flexible models, such as the random forest, are more prone to this? Why can we not detect overfitting if we only look at the training data?
```

Finally, the random forest can also tell us which variables were more useful for making predictions. This is the *variable importance*. It is not the same as the coefficients of a regression, as it does not tell us the direction of the effect, only how much each variable contributed to the predictions.

```{r ml_importance}
tibble(variable = names(model.rf$finalModel$variable.importance),
       importance = model.rf$finalModel$variable.importance) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(variable, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "orange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Importance")
```

```{block, type='alert alert-warning'}
**Question** Which variable is the most important for predicting the commuting flows? Does this match what we found with the gravity models above? Why could it be misleading to treat the importance as the *effect* of the variable?

**Task** Try to improve the predictions of the random forest, e.g. by changing `num.trees` or `min.node.size`, or by adding another explanatory variable. Always evaluate the changes using the *test* data.
```
